item.title: Hackers Pushing Remote Access Tool Through Fake Adobe Acrobat Pages
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers from CloudSEK have uncovered a malicious campaign that uses fake Adobe Acrobat and document-signing web pages to distribute legitimate ConnectWise ScreenConnect remote-access software.

In their research shared with Hackread.com, researchers found that attackers were abusing digitally signed installers configured to connect to unauthorized remote-access tenants, potentially giving external operators persistent access to Windows systems.

This is not the first time criminals have abused ScreenConnect. Hackread.com has previously reported on similar campaigns, including attacks using fake Social Security Administration emails and Word Online pages to distribute ScreenConnect.

However, the latest campaign takes a different approach, using genuine, digitally signed software with attacker-controlled configurations rather than modifying the original binaries.

Fake Pages and Screening Logic

The delivery pages present fake document-review prompts, including titles such as “View & Sign Form” and “Sign in to view document.” When visitors access these pages, scripts check their operating systems and device types, redirecting visitors who are not using Windows desktop systems.

The pages also collect public IP addresses, geolocation, browser, and ISP details before sending them to Telegram bots. They apply ISP-based restrictions that can prevent selected visitors from receiving the download. This filtering may help reduce exposure to automated security analysis, although CloudSEK could not establish its exact purpose.

Visitors who pass the checks automatically receive a ScreenConnect client. One Adobe-themed domain used in the campaign, clickksy.icu, was registered on October 2, 2026, and received a wildcard Let’s Encrypt certificate on the same day. Researchers could not directly retrieve the page because of a Cloudflare challenge.

Configuration and Persistent Access

According to CloudSEK’s report, the threat relies on preconfigured settings inside the installers rather than modified software. The company identified two genuine, digitally signed installers associated with separate ScreenConnect tenants, omydze and vvvzou.

Follow-up collection identified three additional tenant configurations: luminahealthturkey2, tfcconnection, and alunos1. The signatures of those three additional clients were not independently verified.

The two Adobe-associated installers were configured to install ScreenConnect services that launch automatically at startup and run with LocalSystem privileges, according to CloudSEK’s static analysis. This could allow an external operator to maintain remote access to an infected computer.

Operators could then steal data, move across the network, or deploy extra software. CloudSEK noted that “valid vendor signatures do not make a remote-management client safe when it has been configured to connect to an unapproved tenant.”

Advice for Security Teams

CloudSEK has not confirmed any victim compromise or established who operates the infrastructure. The company advises organizations to look beyond file hashes and check their DNS and proxy logs for connections to unknown ScreenConnect servers.

Security teams should also check for unexpected ScreenConnect services on Windows machines and report suspicious tenant IDs to ConnectWise. Restricting ScreenConnect installations to approved tenants can also help prevent unauthorized remote access.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: BITTER APT Using Fake Diplomatic Documents to Deliver PapRAT Spyware
item.description:
Fortinet’s FortiGuard Labs has detailed a cyberespionage campaign targeting South Asian organizations in government, energy, and engineering sectors. The researchers attribute the activity with high confidence to BITTER APT, a suspected South Asian group active since at least 2013.

Infection Chains Explained

FortiGuard Labs identified three chains BITTER uses to deliver a custom remote access trojan (RAT) called PapRAT to Windows systems, and noted that the attackers didn’t rely on exploiting any software vulnerability but focused on deception mostly.

In one chain, attackers used diplomatic- and military-themed LNK shortcuts to launch a script disguised as an icon file through ftp.exe, and relied on living-off-the-land (LotL) techniques. Using built-in Windows utilities such as ftp.exe and curl, along with PowerShell and scheduled tasks, attackers ran commands without initially dropping a conventional malware executable.

The script gathered system and antivirus information and sent the data to a command-and-control (C2) server in a file named abc.pdf. A fake Windows error message helps distract the victim.

The second chain uses a VHDX disk image titled “Letter from the Ambassador – 11th Belt and Road Summit.vhdx.” When mounted, it exposes a shortcut that opens a decoy spreadsheet while launching an MSI installer, Visa_Details.msi, in the background. The installer deploys PapRAT disguised as Microsoft software.

The third chain starts with a RAR archive containing a URL shortcut that retrieves an LNK file through WebDAV. That shortcut eventually launches another MSI installer, Imp_Details.msi, which deploys PapRAT.

PapRAT’s Capabilities

FortiGuard Labs identified PapRAT through build artifacts, including the product name “papsolutions” and the PDB filename “requpap.pdb.” The RAT supports remote command execution, file uploads and downloads, file deletion, directory and drive listing, and screenshot capture.

In the third chain, PapRAT downloads a second implant, WmRAT, disguised as vnces.exe. WmRAT connects to netmansrvdns.com for further commands.

The researchers found C++ and Rust versions of PapRAT. The C++ sample’s C2 configuration is XOR-encoded with key 0x50. The Rust version reverses and ROT-3-shifts strings stored in its .rdata section to conceal its C2 address. It also expands PapRAT’s command set from eight to eleven, adding PowerShell execution, a sleep command, and a clean exit. The Rust variant waits 42 seconds before starting and then checks in every five seconds.

Hackread.com has previously reported on BITTER’s use of malicious archives and custom backdoors in attacks targeting government and military organizations. In April, we also covered the group’s use of ProSpy spyware in a campaign targeting journalists and opposition figures in the Middle East.

The new findings add another part to BITTER’s activity. As researchers noted in the blog post, the campaign shows how BITTER “combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems.” Security teams monitoring targeted sectors must inspect scheduled tasks, scripting tools, and installer activity alongside traditional antivirus signatures to detect these living-off-the-land techniques.

Expert Commentary:

Shane Barney, Chief Information Security Officer at Keeper Security, shared his comments with Hackread.com, stating, “This campaign illustrates how advanced cyberespionage operations deliberately abuse native system tools to evade traditional endpoint detection. By co-opting native Windows utilities like ftp.exe and scheduled tasks to establish initial command-and-control communication, threat actors operate within trusted administrative channels before deploying custom malware.”

“Defending against this hybrid tradecraft requires security teams to focus on strict privilege boundaries and identity security, rather than endpoint signatures alone. Organizations must enforce least-privilege access across all user endpoints, restrict access to native scripting engines, and eliminate standing administrative rights that allow these scripts to execute maliciously,” he added.

Deeba Ahmed

item.title: Guardz Brings Palo Alto Networks Prisma Browser Protection to Small Businesses
item.description:
Miami, United States, November 2nd, 2026, CyberNewswire

Prisma Browser for Business joins Guardz to connect browser protection with email, identity and endpoint security, helping security teams investigate and respond to threats across the workspace

Guardz, the Agentic Workspace Security platform built for managed service providers (MSPs), today announced the integration of Prisma Browser for Business from Palo Alto Networks. The integration connects browser protection with email, identity, endpoint, data and user risk, helping small businesses prevent threats and giving security experts the platform to streamline autonomous unified detection, investigation, and response to incidents across the workspace.

Employees rely on browsers to access business applications, handle company information and use AI tools. But attacks often cross these environments: a phishing email can direct an employee to a fake login page, exposing credentials and putting connected accounts at risk. 

With Prisma Browser for Business built into Guardz, MSPs and the Guardz 24/7 managed detection and response (MDR) team can investigate related activity as a unified incident. If an employee clicks a phishing link, Prisma Browser for Business can block the malicious page, while Guardz correlates the browser event with the original email, related Microsoft 365 activity, and endpoint telemetry to support investigation and response for a single identity.

“Identity is the new center of gravity in cybersecurity, and the browser has become the primary gateway to the modern workspace. Traditional security tools operate in silos, leaving critical gaps in visibility and response,” said Dor Eisner, CEO and Co-Founder of Guardz.

“Together with Palo Alto Networks, we’re advancing a new era of identity-centric security operations, connecting signals across identity, browser, email, endpoint, and data into a unified security fabric that is powered by agents. Guardz enables MSPs to autonomously investigate, correlate, and respond to threats across the entire workspace, while giving small businesses the freedom to embrace AI securely and thrive. This is the future of cybersecurity: identity-centric, unified data fabric, and built for autonomous defense at scale,” Eisner added.

Browser Protection Across the Workspace

Powered by Prisma Browser for Business, the integration brings Palo Alto Networks’ browser security technology into the wider security service MSPs manage through Guardz. Capabilities include:

  • Phishing and session-theft protection: Inline machine-learning phishing detection and Advanced URL Filtering help block malicious pages, including fake login pages and attacks designed to steal live session tokens.
  • Malware and extension security: WildFire file analysis helps detect malicious files, while browser security scans uploads and downloads and identifies risky extensions.
  • Connected investigation and response: Browser events are linked with email, identity and endpoint signals to support incident investigations through Guardz’s 24/7 MDR service.
  • Simplified deployment: Guardz streamlines provisioning, setup and default configuration so MSPs can deploy browser protection within minutes.

The streamlined deployment has also impressed early-access MSPs. “The rollout through our RMM was super smooth. Within minutes, the Prisma Browser for Business extension was on every Chrome and Edge profile, and it was quick and easy to configure and deploy,” said Kevin Kehoe of Datawise Networks.

“For most small businesses, the browser is now the office. Working with Guardz brings Prisma Browser for Business into the security these organizations receive from the providers they already trust. It connects our browser protection with the wider coverage and support their MSP delivers, helping safeguard the applications and information employees use every day,” said Shivam Srivastava, VP Product at Palo Alto Networks.

AI Usage and Control

As employees increasingly use browser-based generative AI tools, small businesses need practical ways to manage which services are permitted and how company information is shared. Guardz AI Usage and Control capabilities let technicians apply client-specific policies, including restrictions on copying, pasting, uploading and downloading files by website or category.

Complementing these controls, Guardz has introduced an AI usage report that gives MSPs a per-client view of AI tool usage based on all signals. The controls help enforce usage policies, while the report provides visibility into adoption.

About Guardz

Guardz delivers Agentic Workspace Security, helping MSPs protect the small businesses they serve. The platform unifies protection across identities, email, endpoints and browsers, alongside adaptive security awareness and user risk, connecting signals around each identity to give security teams the context to act. The Guardz 24/7 agentic MDR provides triage and response at machine speed, supported by an elite research and threat hunting team. Learn more at guardz.com.

About Palo Alto Networks

Palo Alto Networks is the world’s cybersecurity leader. We innovate to outpace cyberthreats, so organizations can embrace technology with confidence. We provide next-gen cybersecurity to thousands of customers globally, across all sectors. Our best-in-class cybersecurity platforms and services are backed by industry-leading threat intelligence and strengthened by state-of-the-art automation. Whether delivering Next-Generation Firewalls, pioneering Agentic AI security, or driving continuous frontier defense via Unit 42, we are committed to helping safely navigate the evolving digital landscape.

Contact

Omri Hurwitz
[email protected]

item.title: How to Keep Your Voice Recordings Private on iPhone
item.description:
What did you last record on your iPhone? A lecture, perhaps, a call with your landlord, or notes from a doctor’s appointment you wanted to remember. Whether you used Apple’s Voice Memos or a recorder app like Voice Recorder+ AI Note Taker, that audio is stored somewhere. Where it is stored, and who can access it, deserves as much attention as the recording itself.

Most of us would happily hand over our browsing history before our voice memos. A recording has your voice, other people’s voices, names, numbers, and sometimes a home address read aloud. And yet we treat these files like sticky notes. Record, forget, never delete. 

There’s a newer reason to care, too. Voice cloning tools have gotten scarily good, and they need exactly what a long, clean recording of you talking provides. Not a reason to panic. Just a reason not to leave hours of your voice lying around in folders you forgot existed.  None of this takes long to fix, though. Most of it is settings you flip once. 

Where Your Recordings Actually Go 

Short answer: more places than you’d guess. A recording starts on the phone. But if you use Voice Memos with iCloud switched on, it also shows up on every Apple device signed in to the same account. Super convenient, right up until you remember the old iPad your family still passes around. 

File names leak stuff too. With Location-based Naming turned on, Voice Memos names each new recording after where you made it. Send “Recording at 18 Elm Street” to a group chat and, well, you’ve shared a bit more than audio. 

Then there’s transcription. Loads of apps turn speech into text now, and plenty of them do it by uploading your audio to a server somewhere. That’s not automatically bad. You just want to know when it happens, whether the file sticks around afterwards, and whether it’s used to train anything. If the privacy policy dances around those three, that’s kind of your answer. 

Pick the App Before You Need It 

Most people choose a recording app in a panic, about five seconds before a meeting starts. Better to decide while you’re calm. Here’s what I’d look for: 

  • a plain-English note on what leaves the device and when 
  • exports in normal formats (MP3, M4A, WAV), so you’re not stuck 
  • folders, so the sensitive stuff isn’t sitting next to your grocery lists 
  • recordings saved on the phone by default, not pushed to someone else’s cloud 

The model you want is basically “local first, cloud only when I ask.” Whatever app you end up with, check that one thing. 

Also worth a look: can you lock the app with Face ID or a passcode? And when you delete a recording, is it actually gone, or does it hang around in a “recently deleted” folder for weeks? Small stuff, but it adds up. 

A VPN Helps. Just Not Where You’d Think 

“Use a VPN and you’re safe” leaves out several risks when handling audio recordings. HTTPS already encrypts a recording while it travels from an app to its server. A VPN can also hide destination addresses and DNS requests from the local Wi-Fi operator, depending on its configuration.

That can help when uploading interviews from a café, hotel or airport, but it does not control how the recording app stores, processes or shares your audio once it arrives.

One practical thing. Big audio files take a while to upload, WAV especially, so the upload is often still crawling along while you’re halfway out the café door. Keep the VPN on until it finishes, instead of only while the app is open on your screen. 

What a VPN can’t do is fix storage. A recording sitting in a shared Drive folder behind a public link is exposed no matter how carefully you connected when you uploaded it. So my order of priorities goes: storage first, sharing second, network third. 

The Legal Bit Nobody Reads 

Recording other people comes with rules, and they change depending on where you are. In California, for example, recording a confidential conversation without everyone’s consent can cost up to $2,500 per violation under Penal Code 632. A bunch of other US states also want everyone on board, and lots of countries have their own versions. 

The easy fix? Ask out loud at the start. “Mind if I record this?” You get permission, and the “yes” ends up right there on the tape. Nice little bonus. 

A Ten-Minute Cleanup 

If you’ve never looked at your recordings with privacy in mind, start here: 

  1. Turn off location-based file names. 
  2. Lock the Voice Memos App (iOS 18 or later)
  3. Check which recordings sync to iCloud, and which devices can see them. 
  4. Delete audio you’ve already transcribed and don’t need anymore. 
  5. Dig up old recordings you shared in chats and get rid of copies nobody needs. 
  6. Set a passcode if you somehow don’t have one. iOS file encryption leans on it. 

Honestly, most leaks from recordings aren’t hacks at all. They’re a file forwarded once too often, into a group chat nobody remembers joining. 

(Photo by Amanz on Unsplash)

  4. Delete audio you’ve already transcribed and don’t need anymore. 
  5. Dig up old recordings you shared in chats and get rid of copies nobody needs. 
  6. Set a passcode if you somehow don’t have one. iOS file encryption leans on it. 

Honestly, most leaks from recordings aren’t hacks at all. They’re a file forwarded once too often, into a group chat nobody remembers joining.

item.title: Cogent Security Makes the Fortune Cyber 60 for a Second Year, With a Plan to Run Cyber Defense Like a Factory
item.description:
San Francisco, CA, November 3rd, 2026, CyberNewswire

Cogent Security, an applied AI cybersecurity company, reported that the PHP2Shell vulnerability exposed significant gaps in enterprise vulnerability response. Disclosed on October 21, PHP2Shell involved two critical flaws that had remained in PHP for more than a decade. AI-assisted research helped identify the vulnerabilities and develop working exploits in approximately one week, with attacks beginning before a patch was available. Cloudflare recorded millions of exploitation attempts that day.

According to Cogent Security’s research, by 5 p.m. Pacific, the average Fortune 500 company had patched fewer than 1% of its 2,266 affected assets.

That gap between how fast attackers move and how fast large companies respond is the problem Cogent was built to close. The company, an applied AI lab focused on cybersecurity, has been named to the Fortune Cyber 60 for the second consecutive year.

The list, developed by Fortune with Lightspeed Venture Partners and AWS, recognizes 60 of the most important venture-backed cybersecurity startups that have yet to go public, be acquired, or reach another significant exit, grouped by stage. Selection weighs financial performance, growth, business operations, and cybersecurity market research, and Fortune validates the final list. 

“Attackers already run like a factory. AI is finding the bugs and writing the exploits, and in some cases it’s running most of the attack,” said Vineet Edupuganti, Cogent’s co-founder and CEO. “Most enterprises are still defending by hand, one ticket and one handoff at a time. Making this list two years in a row tells us security leaders are ready to change how that work gets done.”

The attackers built their factories first

Edupuganti borrows an analogy from manufacturing. Factories replaced the lone skilled worker with a production line, and the most advanced plants now run largely on their own while people design the line and handle the exceptions. Offense, he argues, has already made that shift.

The data points the same way. Google’s M-Trends 2026 report estimates the mean time to exploit at negative seven days, which means exploitation now routinely begins before a fix exists. Researchers have shown AI producing working exploits for newly published vulnerabilities in about 15 minutes, at roughly a dollar apiece. In a state-sponsored campaign that Anthropic disrupted, AI agents carried out 80 to 90% of the tactical work.

Enterprise defense still moves at the pace of its slowest handoff. When PHP2Shell landed, security teams had to find every asset running PHP, including base images and forgotten servers, then work out which were internet-facing and which the business depended on. After that came owners, tickets, change windows, and a rescan to confirm each fix held, with every step falling to a skilled person with a tool.

Building the Defender’s Production Line

Cogent’s answer is what it calls the Cyber Defense Factory, an operating model in which AI agents take over the work that now moves by hand between security tools, while people set the policies those agents follow. The company sells an enterprise platform for autonomous cyber defense, and its first product applies the model to vulnerability management.

The line starts with an inventory. Agents build one deduplicated record of every asset across cloud, on-premises and endpoint environments, inferring each one’s owner and business importance from systems the company already keeps. Findings flow in from the scanners and security tools customers already run, and Cogent matches newly published vulnerabilities against its live software inventory so exposure surfaces before scanners catch up. Agents then check whether the vulnerable software is running and reachable, and they write out the reasoning behind every priority.

Cogent groups remediation work by fix, so one patch can resolve a vulnerability across dozens of servers. Inside the autonomy zones each customer defines, agents carry out supported fixes on their own. On managed endpoints, for instance, they write the remediation script, push it through the company’s existing endpoint management platform, and read back the results. Changes outside those zones go to a single owner as a ticket and wait for a person’s approval, and Cogent closes the work only after the next scan confirms the fix held.

The company says the goal is for enterprises to transform their cybersecurity functions with a factory model to do 100 times more work, 100 times faster. Most customers start with agents in an assistive role and widen their authority as the results earn trust, an approach Cogent calls progressive autonomy.

PHP2Shell gave the model a live test. Cogent’s Zero Day Response processed the advisory and mapped vulnerable assets across customer environments in an average of five minutes, days before scanner signatures were available. Applied to the average Fortune 500 environment in Cogent’s research, the analysis cut 2,266 affected assets down to 16 that had PHP loaded at runtime, faced the internet, and supported critical business functions. That shortlist was waiting for security teams when they sat down to start work.

A Lab With Its Own Models

Cogent describes itself as an applied AI lab that just happens to focus on defensive cybersecurity, and the label reflects how the company is built. It is the only cybersecurity company that trains and deploys its own frontier reasoning models for security use cases. Its domain-specific model, VR-1, has topped cybersecurity benchmarks, outperforming general-purpose frontier models on security tasks.

The model works alongside Cogent’s Context Engine, which ties each vulnerability to the assets, identities, applications, owners, and dependencies around it. That context usually sits scattered across asset databases, ticket histories and architecture documents, and pulling it together is what lets agents judge which changes are safe to make.

“A general-purpose AI model knows a little about everything,” Edupuganti said. “When an AI agent is deciding whether a patch is safe to push to a few thousand production servers, it needs a model that has learned how vulnerabilities, exploits and enterprise systems behave, plus deep context on the company it’s protecting. Put those together and you can give agents real responsibility.”

Racing the Exploit Clock

For security leaders, Edupuganti argues, the number that matters now is the time between a vulnerability’s disclosure and a verified fix, and that window has to be shorter than the time an attacker needs to build and launch an exploit. Cogent is betting that closing it takes a different operating model, one where security work grows with the production line rather than with headcount.

The company’s second straight appearance on the Cyber 60 suggests buyers are warming to that bet, though Edupuganti expects people to stay at the center of it.

“The most advanced factories still have people in them. They decide what the line builds and the standard it holds,” he said. “Security teams are moving into that role. They set the policy and make the judgment calls, and the agents do the work at machine speed.”

About Cogent

Cogent Security is an applied AI lab building the enterprise platform for autonomous cyber defense. Its AI agents find and fix vulnerabilities at machine speed so every enterprise can run its own Cyber Defense Factory. Starting with autonomous vulnerability management, Cogent carries vulnerabilities from disclosure to a verified fix across cloud, on-premises, and endpoint environments, identifying exposure within minutes and confirming what attackers can reach along the way. Customers set the policies the agents follow and decide which fixes run autonomously and which wait for approval. Fortune 500 security teams using Cogent have reduced the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97 percent. Built by researchers and operators from Google DeepMind, Abnormal Security, and Coinbase, Cogent is backed by Greylock Partners and Bain Capital Ventures. Learn more at cogent.com.

Ignacio Ramirez

item.title: Cursor Distributed Claude Code Extensions With SSH Backdoor Code
item.description:
Developers installing Claude Code through Cursor’s extension marketplace were offered tampered packages designed to collect information about their computers and give attackers remote access. Cursor removed the malicious downloads but warned that deleting the extension alone will not remove the files it left behind.

The company published its security notice on October 29, 2026, then updated it on October 30 to identify two affected versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, for Windows and macOS. The packages were available between approximately 2.27 am and 1.35 pm Pacific Daylight Time on October 29, equivalent to 9.27 am to 8.35 pm GMT

Malicious Code Ran Before the Extension Started

OpenSourceMalware’s analysis of version 2.1.313 found a 66-line malicious loader inserted before the extension’s normal JavaScript code. The package retained the legitimate extension identity anthropic.claude-code, and included the genuine bundled binary.

The malicious loader executed before the extension’s normal code. OpenSourceMalware reported that it ran when the extension activated after startup or when its webview opened. The researchers identified the altered extension.js file as the difference from the normal package.

Microsoft’s separate investigation confirmed that the malicious packages were not distributed through its Visual Studio Marketplace or the Claude Code npm package. Anthropic also told Microsoft that its systems had not been compromised and that it had not developed the malicious package.

SSH Access Attempts Did Not Succeed on Every Computer

Once running, the loader gathered information about the host and user before attempting to add an attacker-controlled SSH key, enable SSH and create a reverse tunnel. Such a tunnel can provide a connection from an affected computer to an external server, allowing remote access when the necessary services and permissions are available.

Cursor said coding errors and administrator-permission requirements blocked the SSH access step on most Windows and macOS computers. However, the package could still leave tvflcf an unauthorised key, startup files, and transmitted device information. A failed tunnel therefore did not mean the installation required no cleanup.

Microsoft also identified startup mechanisms outside the extension’s installation directory. These included a macOS LaunchAgent, a Windows scheduled task named SysMon and a fallback script in the Windows Startup folder. Its analysis distinguishes what the code attempted from what investigators could confirm had succeeded on an individual computer.

Removing the Extension Is Only Part of the Cleanup

Cursor temporarily closed the marketplace, rotated keys and rebuilt it before restoring service. It also worked with the hosting provider to take the attacker’s server offline.

Affected users should follow the detection and remediation instructions in the official notice, remove the unauthorised SSH key and persistence files, and rotate accessible credentials from a trusted computer. Cursor provides separate cleanup scripts for Windows and macOS and advises assessing whether affected computers need to be rebuilt.

Editor’s note: Cursor’s initial notice said at most 5,000 users were affected. That figure has since been removed, and the updated notice identifies version 2.1.312 alongside 2.1.313. The original notice is available through the Internet Archive.

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: What to Know Before Getting a Crypto Debit Card
item.description:
Even if you haven’t been a staunch supporter, it is hard to ignore the impact that cryptocurrency has had on the global financial market. Most are familiar with the behemoth that is Bitcoin, but there are thousands of other crypto options out there now.

In fact, you can even get a crypto Visa card from a litany of established financial institutions. But before you run out to get your own crypto debit card, there are a few important things that you should keep in mind so that you can use it to your fullest advantage.

Traditional vs. Crypto

The concept of a debit card across either form of currency is much the same. That said, there are key differences. One of the biggest benefits to using a crypto debit card is that you may not be subject to global currency conversion rates.

Then again, there are a number of avenues that crypto debit cards don’t have access to that traditional debit cards do. The differences are oftentimes small, but they can matter from person to person. You might not need a bank account to use a crypto debit card, but you may run into availability issues when it comes to vendors.

Is it an Option in Your Area?

The internet has made the global community tighter than ever before, but the local community is even more vital. If you plan on getting a crypto debit card, it is important to have a good idea of where you can use it and to be familiar with current regulations before signing up.

For instance, do many of your local establishments take it as an accepted form of payment? What online vendors allow you to use them? Though crypto acceptance has grown exponentially, it still isn’t on the same level as traditional debit and credit cards just yet.

Fees and Exchange Rates

Exchange rates – and, no, that doesn’t mean country to country – are at play when using a crypto debit card. There are two ways the card works: it either directly converts your crypto into a fiat currency (U.S. dollars, for instance) or you pre-load the card using your crypto funds.

Banks and financial institutions often have fees associated with this. They may be nominal – and some institutions may even waive those fees – but they do exist. Make sure you know how much it is going to cost to convert your crypto, not to mention what kind of rates may be involved in the conversion process.

Know the Tax Implications

Though it can sound like a headache, there are potential tax implications attached to using a crypto debit card in most parts of the world. For instance, the United States classifies cryptocurrency as a capital asset (property), meaning capital gains and losses must be declared.

This can all get quite confusing, quite fast. Take some time to make yourself familiar with crypto tax regulations. When all else fails, talk to a crypto tax expert to know what preparations you must make before signing up for and using a crypto debit card. Being prepared can save you a lot of hassle when it comes to your taxes.

Know How Crypto Debit Cards Work

It can be all too easy to get caught up in crypto mania, but know what you are getting into first. Crypto debit cards can allow you to make the most of your crypto holdings in the short term, but you should be educated first to know if that is the best move for your current financial goals. It is an exciting time in finance, but don’t forget to cover your bases.

Disclosure: This article was published in collaboration with Utorg and does not constitute financial or investment advice.

(Photo by Dmytro Demidko on Unsplash)

item.title: 3AM Ransomware Hits 37 UK School Systems in Suspected AI-Assisted Attack
item.description:
Cybersecurity firm Bitdefender has investigated what it believes is Europe’s first ransomware incident involving a human operator and suspected AI-driven command retries.

In research shared with Hackread.com ahead of its publication, the cybersecurity firm detailed how a 3AM (ThreeAM) ransomware affiliate breached a UK school estate with 47 systems across separate Active Directory domains and encrypted about 37 machines.

Human Decisions, Automated Retries

In its blog post, published today, Bitdefender described the intrusion as “a hybrid operation in which some parts show a human operator at the keyboard while others behave like an agentic loop.” The suspected loop fed command results back to a language model, which then suggested alternative commands.

The timing supports that interpretation: key steps were minutes apart, while failed commands were retried every 40 to 101 seconds. However, Bitdefender could not confirm whether a model was running the loop automatically or whether an operator was copying commands and results between a terminal and an AI tool.

The distinction matters. This was not a confirmed autonomous ransomware attack. The evidence points to possible AI assistance within an operation that still relied on conventional intrusion techniques.

The affiliate mainly used living-off-the-land techniques, relying on Windows tools such as PowerShell, WMI, netsh, reg and rundll32. It also used public tools, including Mimikatz and Impacket-style remote execution, alongside the 3AM encryptor. As Bitdefender noted, AI-enabled attacks do not need novel tools to succeed.

Domain Trusts and Ransomware Deployment

The attacker stole backup credentials on September 10 and 11 using scripts that decrypted stored passwords with Windows DPAPI and copied browser credentials. Mimikatz was downloaded on September 12, then renamed to sysmon64.exe. On September 14, the attacker dumped registry hives and created backdoor administrator accounts named library and svc_bkpmon.

On September 15, files from a finance share were staged in Windows registry values and transferred through an unmanaged machine used as command-and-control infrastructure.

On September 18, the attacker used dnscmd to create DNS conditional forwarders, then netdom to establish two-way trusts between separate domains. Diagnostic scripts, including wb_probe, ran trust-verification commands, but Bitdefender could not determine what the probes returned. Netlogon was restarted later that day. A scheduled PowerShell task then pushed the backdoor account’s access to about 40 machines.

The following day, attempts to remove Sophos and Bitdefender endpoint protection were blocked by anti-tampering controls. The attacker deployed a script loader before running the Rust-based 3AM encryptor, which encrypted about 37 systems and deleted system-state backups with wbadmin.

The findings raise a practical concern for defenders. Even if AI helped troubleshoot the attack, the damage came through familiar weaknesses involving credentials, domain trust and backup protection, and Bitdefender expects hybrid attacks to become more common in 2027.

Researchers recommend that defenders should start separating privileged accounts across domains, monitoring new domain trusts, protecting backup infrastructure and ensuring every machine has endpoint protection.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

The findings raise a practical concern for defenders. Even if AI helped troubleshoot the attack, the damage came through familiar weaknesses involving credentials, domain trust and backup protection, and Bitdefender expects hybrid attacks to become more common in 2027.

Researchers recommend that defenders should start separating privileged accounts across domains, monitoring new domain trusts, protecting backup infrastructure and ensuring every machine has endpoint protection.

item.title: Binance Hack: Fake Job Interviews Helped Hackers Steal $6.34 Billion
item.description:
Binance explains how North Korean hackers used fake job interviews, malicious developer tools and an internal AI tool in its $6.34 billion cryptocurrency theft.

Binance says a fake job interview process and abuse of an internal AI tool helped attackers reach its wallet infrastructure before the October 29, 2026 theft of $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency. Its initial incident report, published on November 3, traces the campaign through the compromised devices of three engineers.

As Hackread.com previously reported, the FBI attributed the attack to North Korea.

The exchange has stated that it would cover the financial losses. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng addressed concerns over the financial impact in a statement on X, saying, “We are committed to covering all hacked losses through our company funds. Your assets are safe.”

Fake Recruitment Led to Wallet Access

In its latest incident report, Binance traced the campaign back to June, when a wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while searching for an AI coding tool. Although Binance detected the activity, replaced the device and rotated credentials, the attackers learned the employee’s role and connections within the wallet team.

In September, another engineer, identified as Engineer B, was approached through a job-hunting platform by someone posing as a recruiter. The second interview ended with Engineer B being asked to download a coding assignment onto his work laptop.

Binance says the repository contained malware that replaced a legitimate pyenv file with a malicious one, giving attackers a way to run their own commands on the machine and contact a server they controlled.

On October 20, the attackers used Engineer B’s compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain access to the devices of Engineer A and another wallet engineer, identified as Engineer C. Engineer A’s computer held a container deployment token. Binance has not explained how the AI tool enabled that access.

Attackers Abused Ethereum’s Authorization Mechanism

On October 29, the attackers accessed Engineer C’s computer and used credentials stolen from Engineer A to deploy a container and launch a malicious script. Between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC, five Binance hot wallets transferred 233.46 million XRP. Wallets on Solana and Optimism subsequently sent approximately 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP, followed by 18,270 BTC.

The attackers also abused Ethereum’s EIP-7702 account-authorization mechanism, which allows an account to delegate certain execution rights to a smart contract. This gave an attacker-controlled contract partial execution rights over a Binance hot wallet without exposing its private key.

Suspending withdrawals could not immediately stop these on-chain authorizations. Binance said its multi-party computation (MPC) wallet setup meant there was no single private key available to revoke them immediately.

The exchange acknowledged the difficulty in its incident report, stating, “These challenges extended the time required to fully contain the unauthorized asset movements.”

The final unauthorized transfer, involving 2,961.9 ETH, settled at 23:56 UTC after having been broadcast earlier and remaining pending. Binance cleared the malicious delegation at 00:10 UTC on October 30.

As of its November 3 report, Binance said approximately $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted, with the figure subject to reconciliation and market price changes. Separately, it said 98% of the affected token assets had been replenished by October 31.

That replenishment represents replacement assets, not the recovery of 98% of the stolen funds. Binance said it had rebuilt affected systems, replaced compromised devices and tightened access controls. The investigation remains ongoing, and independent cybersecurity firms will review its findings.

This incident follows another major North Korean-linked crypto theft. In February 2025, attackers stole approximately $1.5 billion from Bybit in an operation the FBI attributed to North Korea. Hackread.com reported on the theft and the subsequent investigation linking it to the Lazarus Group.

Commenting on Binance’s findings, Gina Cardelli, Director of Platform and Threat Intelligence at Fortra, questioned how the compromised employee device enabled access to sensitive systems.

“My questions would be around the security controls surrounding that employee’s environment. “An engineer seeking a new job downloaded a malicious coding assignment, giving attackers a foothold in a campaign that ultimately gained access to the company’s wallets. While using a work computer for an external coding assessment warrants its own scrutiny, the larger concern is how that compromise enabled access to other systems and sensitive financial infrastructure.”

(Photo by Bastian Riccardi)

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: The Sandbox Fights Back: Joe Security Launches Adaptive Detonation
item.description:
Reinach, Switzerland, November 4th, 2026, CyberNewswire

AI agents help Joe Sandbox uncover malicious behavior concealed by evasion techniques and unmet execution conditions.

Joe Security‘s Adaptive Detonation brings active intervention to malware analysis, helping security teams investigate threats that may conceal their behavior during an initial sandbox run.

Adaptive Detonation uses AI agents to examine execution results, identify obstacles preventing a sample from revealing relevant behavior, and select targeted interventions. These can include patching a blocking check, creating required files or settings, adjusting the execution environment, or supplying missing command-line arguments.

Joe Sandbox then analyzes the sample again under the modified conditions to verify whether the intervention reveals additional activity.

The approach addresses obstacles including keyboard restrictions, timing checks, firmware-based rejection, date requirements, and missing dependencies. By connecting observed evidence with targeted action and verification, Adaptive Detonation helps analysts investigate why a sample remains inactive and uncover behavior that might otherwise stay hidden.

For security teams, this means deeper visibility into evasive threats and more evidence to support investigations.

Adaptive Detonation is available as part of Joe Sandbox AI, a plugin for Joe Sandbox Cloud. Security teams can test Joe Sandbox by signing in or registering for Joe Sandbox Cloud Basic, the free community version.

Read the Adaptive Detonation blog post for technical details, malware case studies, and original and follow-up analysis reports.

About Joe Security

Joe Security is a privately owned Swiss software company founded in 2011 and headquartered in Reinach, Switzerland. It develops malware and phishing analysis technology, combining dynamic analysis, agentic reverse engineering and dedicated analyst lab environments.

Contact

VP
Marius Fitigau
